Inside the ML Layer · Part 8 · Agents

The Top of the Stack: Agent Runtimes, Tool Protocols and the Software That Lets Models Act

A model on its own only produces text. An agent runtime wraps it in a loop: decide, call a tool, read the result, decide again, until the task is done. Around that loop sit protocols that connect models to tools (MCP) and to other agents (A2A), frameworks that structure the work, sandboxes that keep code execution safe, and tracing that shows what happened. This final part of the series explains that top layer, and how agents feed back into every layer below.

3. The agent loop

Almost every agent, however elaborate, is the loop the ReAct paper described in 2022: the model reasons, chooses an action, the runtime executes it and returns an observation, and the model continues. The runtime's job is everything the model cannot do itself: run tools, keep state, stop runaway loops, retry failures, ask a human when needed, and keep the context window from overflowing by summarising or dropping old material ("compaction").

4. Tool calling, from model to engine

Tool use starts in training: models are post-trained (Part 5) to emit structured calls, a tool name plus JSON arguments matching a schema. The serving engine (Part 7) can enforce the schema with constrained decoding, masking tokens that would break the JSON, which SGLang and vLLM support. Models can now request several calls at once ("parallel tool calls"), and the runtime runs them concurrently. Because every tool definition sits in the prompt, large tool sets cost tokens on every call; runtimes increasingly load tools on demand.

5. MCP and A2A

MCP: Model Context ProtocolReleased by Anthropic in November 2024. A client (in the AI app) talks to servers that expose tools, resources (data) and prompts, using JSON-RPC over stdio for local servers or streamable HTTP for remote ones. Adopted by Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor and others; over 10,000 servers by late 2025. Donated to the Linux Foundation's new Agentic AI Foundation on 9 Dec 2025, alongside Block's goose and OpenAI's AGENTS.md.
A2A: Agent2AgentAnnounced by Google in April 2025 for agents to discover each other (via "agent cards"), delegate tasks and exchange results, whoever built them. Moved to the Linux Foundation in June 2025 with backers including AWS, Cisco, Microsoft, Salesforce, SAP and ServiceNow. Complements MCP: MCP connects an agent to tools; A2A connects agents to agents.

Why a protocol: N × M versus N + M

Without a shared protocol, every AI app needs a custom integration for every tool. With one, each side implements the protocol once.

⚠️ The security catchProtocols make it easy to connect tools, including untrusted ones. Prompt injection (instructions hidden in a web page, email or file the agent reads) and tool poisoning (malicious tool descriptions) can steer an agent into leaking data or taking actions its user never asked for. Defences are partly in the runtime: least-privilege permissions, human approval for sensitive actions, isolating untrusted content, and allow-listing servers.

7. The frameworks

    

    

    
Two camps have formed. The lab SDKs (OpenAI's, Anthropic's, Google's) are thin and opinionated, built around their own models and hosted tools, though most accept other models. The independent frameworks (LangGraph, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, Microsoft's) are model-agnostic and add orchestration, state and integrations. All have converged on the same primitives: tools, handoffs or sub-agents, guardrails, memory, MCP support and tracing.

9. Sandboxes and isolation

    
Agents that write and run code, browse or control computers must be isolated from the systems they run on. Options trade isolation strength against start-up time and overhead. AWS built Firecracker (paper at NSDI 2020) for Lambda; its specification targets about 125 ms from start to the guest's init process with under 5 MiB of memory overhead, and it underlies several agent-sandbox services.

10. Agents at AI-factory scale

    
Agents change the economics of everything below them. One task can mean dozens of model calls, each re-sending a growing context, so prefix caching (Part 7) becomes essential: most of each call is identical to the last. Long-running agents hold KV cache for minutes, shifting serving toward memory. And every agent run is potential training data: agentic RL (Part 5) trains models on exactly these loops, judged by agent evaluations (Part 6).

    

      
What does one agent task cost?

      
Our own model: context grows linearly each step; cached input is billed at a discount. Prices are inputs, not quotes.

      

      

      

      

      

      

      

    


    
11. Observability and safety

    
    
      
  • Tracing: each agent run becomes a tree of spans (agent invocation, model calls, tool executions). OpenTelemetry's GenAI semantic conventions define span types such as invoke_agent and execute_tool; they are still in development, and vendor tools (LangSmith, Langfuse, Arize, the lab SDKs' built-in tracing) fill the gap.
    • 
      
  • Guardrails: input and output checks that run alongside the agent and can stop it; built into the OpenAI Agents SDK and others.
    • 
      
  • Permissions: which tools an agent may call without asking, with human approval for destructive or external actions.
    • 
      
  • Evaluation: agent benchmarks and production replays (Part 6) catch regressions when models, prompts or tools change.
    •

VerdictThe agent layer is the youngest and fastest-moving in the stack, but it has settled faster than expected: one loop, one tool protocol (MCP) now under neutral governance, one agent-to-agent protocol (A2A), and frameworks converging on the same primitives. The hard problems have moved to reliability, security and cost: keeping agents on task over hundreds of steps, defending against injected instructions, and making long contexts cheap. Those problems are solved as much in the layers below (training, evaluation, serving) as in the runtime itself.


    
13. The whole stack

    

      
Inside the ML Layer: the series map

      
Eight parts, from the top of the stack to the GPU. Tap to open a part.

      

    

    
An agent answering a question touches every layer in this series: its runtime calls a model served by an inference engine using kernels on GPUs, a model that was post-trained with RL, checked by evaluation harnesses, trained with parallelism libraries on a framework. Part 1's trace followed that path from the bottom; this series has now opened each box. The companion series, Inside the Data Layer, follows the data that feeds them.
